intro.why: "If you don't build logging and error handling into your system, your users will become your loggers." Robust, clean, shareable code is what turns a promising notebook into a service others can trust.

symbols: single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion

sections.title: Errors and failing fast
sections.plain: Detect bad input early, loudly, before it silently corrupts results.
sections.body:
Robustness: code must not behave unexpectedly when given incorrect input. Fail early: detect errors before they silently corrupt data. Data science is domain-specific: missing values or outliers can trigger logic errors rather than crashes. Error handling protects pipeline integrity; fail fast rather than continue with bad state.

ExceptionTypical ML cause
ValueErrorIncompatible array shapes; invalid parameter values
KeyErrorMissing DataFrame column
TypeErrorPassing a string to a numeric function
IndexErrorIndex out of range

sections.title: Handling errors: specific and custom exceptions, tracebacks
sections.plain: Catch exactly what you expect, explain it, and define your own error types.
sections.body:
Specific exceptions: catch FileNotFoundError, ValueError… not a bare except:, which also catches KeyboardInterrupt and MemoryError and can leave a "zombie" process. Give meaningful messages. Define custom exceptions for domain errors (e.g. InvalidFeatureConfigError, IncompatibleFeatureSizeError, ModelWeightsNotLoadedError, each inheriting from Exception or a more specific built-in). Where appropriate, log and return a predictable default.

Reading tracebacks: bottom to top. The last line gives the error type and message; the lines above are the chain of calls, with file names and line numbers.

Debugging process
  1. Reproduce the error.
  2. Locate it (traceback, logs).
  3. Identify the root cause.
  4. Fix it.
  5. Test the fix.
  6. Document it.

sections.title: Logging, log levels and debugging strategies
sections.plain: Persistent, categorised, timestamped records beat print statements.
sections.body:
Why logging beats print: persistent history (a 48-hour training job on a cloud VM crashes at hour 40: the log survives, a closed terminal doesn't); categorisation by level, so you can filter by severity; contextual metadata (timestamps, module names, line numbers); and shipping to central tools (CloudWatch, Elasticsearch).

LevelUse for
DEBUGDetailed troubleshooting information
INFORoutine milestones (model loaded)
WARNINGUnexpected but non-fatal (feature missing, using default)
ERRORAn operation failed
CRITICAL / FATALSystem crash; cannot continue

Demo (error handling and logging): a model expecting 3 features; scenario 1 clean data → prediction logged at INFO; scenario 2 dimension mismatch → WARNING and fallback 0.00; scenario 3 missing data (NaN) → ERROR "data corruption", halting for that record. Code example ex1 reproduces this.

Debugging strategies: rubber ducking (explain the code line by line), divide and conquer (shrink to the smallest failing example), and debuggers (pdb, IDE breakpoints).

sections.title: Style, formatting, linting and type checking
sections.plain: Consistent style, automated; types checked before running.
sections.body:
"Code is read much more often than it is written" (Guido van Rossum). PEP 8: consistency and automation. Naming: snake_case for variables and functions, PascalCase for classes. Indentation: 4 spaces, never tabs. Spaces around operators. Imports grouped (standard library, third-party, local), separated by blank lines.

Black: a zero-configuration formatter that rewrites code to PEP 8; saves time, eliminates style merge conflicts, lets reviews focus on logic.

Linters: Ruff (very fast, all-in-one), Flake8, Pylint: flag unused variables and imports, unreachable code and non-compliant names.

Type hints + mypy: def scale(data: List[float], factor: float) -> List[float]: return [x * factor for x in data]. Self-documenting, better IDE support, and static checking catches type errors before runtime.

sections.title: Research code vs production code
sections.plain: Notebooks for discovery; modules, tests and config for services.
sections.body:
ResearchProduction
GoalDiscovery, proof of conceptRepeatable, robust service
ToolsJupyter.py scripts, containers
PrioritySpeed of insightStability, scalability
ProcessManual, interactiveAutomated CI/CD
Unit of workNotebook cellModular function or class
Error handlingManual inspectionLogging and exceptions
TestingVisual plottingUnit and integration tests
ConfigurationHard-codedYAML or environment config
StateInteractive, globalLocal, encapsulated

The hidden-state problem: cells run out of order (cell 5, then cell 3) produce results nobody can reproduce; notebooks are JSON and hard to version; globals leak between cells. Move verified logic into modules.

sections.title: Refactoring, code smells and SOLID for ML
sections.plain: Improve structure without changing behaviour; depend on abstractions.
sections.body:
Refactoring: changing internal structure without changing external behaviour.

PrincipleIn ML code
S: single responsibilityOne function, one task (e.g. only cleaning)
O: open/closedOpen for extension (new model types), closed for modification
L: Liskov substitutionAny model subclass can replace the base without breaking callers
I: interface segregationSmall focused interfaces (a predictor needn't implement training)
D: dependency inversionDepend on abstractions, not concrete classes

Modularity: split a monolithic train_and_predict() into data_loader.py, preprocessor.py, model_trainer.py, evaluator.py.

Dependency inversion: bad: load_data() creates SQLDatabase().fetch("SELECT * FROM table") inside. Good: load_data(source: DataSource) calls source.get_all(), so SQL, CSV or S3 sources can be swapped (and tests can pass a fake).

Code smells: long functions, duplicated logic, large "god" classes, hard-coded paths. Refactorings: extract function (scale_features()), rename variables (user_demographics_df, random_forest_model), replace magic numbers (OUTLIER_THRESHOLD = 3.0), modularise into utils.py/preprocessing.py. A refactor must give the same output: in the demo both the monolithic and refactored versions predict 75.0.

sections.title: APIs for ML services: FastAPI and validation
sections.plain: Wrap the model in a web API with a strict input schema.
sections.body:
Model-as-a-service: decouples the model from the UI; any language can call it; scales independently (e.g. on GPUs); models can be updated seamlessly. Communication is REST + JSON.

Inference service: an endpoint (/v1/predict), a JSON payload of features, validation against a schema, and a response (confidence, classes or values). A typical stack: FastAPI service + model file + a database (e.g. PostgreSQL) for storing predictions + any HTTP client UI.

FastAPI: high performance (built on Starlette), automatic interactive docs (Swagger/OpenAPI at /docs), type safety via Pydantic, async support and type hints.

class InputData(BaseModel):
    age: int = Field(..., gt=0, lt=120)
    income: float
    zip_code: str

Invalid requests get HTTP 422 Unprocessable Content with a list of errors, before the model is called (customer-churn prediction demo). Code example ex2 tests valid and invalid payloads in-process.

sections.title: Version control for data science
sections.plain: Sharing equals reproducibility: track code, review changes, keep data out of Git.
sections.body: Sharing is reproducibility. Git for data science: track changes, use feature branches, review via pull requests, and add large datasets and .ipynb_checkpoints to .gitignore. A branching strategy maps to environments (dev, UAT, prod). Never commit large data or models: use DVC (Session M6).

sections.title: Dependencies, packaging and Docker
sections.plain: Pin what you depend on, package what you share, containerise what you run.
sections.body:
Dependency management: always use virtual environments. requirements.txt (simple, legacy); Conda/Mamba (manages non-Python libraries such as C++ and GPU drivers); Poetry (deterministic: poetry.lock pins transitive dependencies).

Python packages: a src/mypackage/ layout with pyproject.toml (or legacy setup.py), published to a private index (PyPI mirror, Artifactory) so colleagues can pip install my_internal_ml_lib.

Docker for ML ends "works on my machine": it bundles OS, drivers (CUDA) and code, giving identical training and production environments and portability.

FROM python:3.9-slim
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . /app
CMD ["python", "/app/serve.py"]

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Don't log secrets or personal data; logs are widely readable and retained.
  • Structured (JSON) logs make searching and alerting far easier than free text.
  • Validate at boundaries (API input, file load, feature store read) and trust internal calls.
  • Copy requirements first in a Dockerfile so dependency layers are cached when only code changes (Session M12).

code.title: Specific and custom exceptions with logging
code.explain: Custom exceptions for feature-size and unloaded-weights errors; safe_predict logs INFO for success, WARNING plus a fallback for a recoverable mismatch, and ERROR for NaN input; a bare except swallows even SystemExit.
mistakes: print() instead of logging in long jobs.
code.notes: Configure logging once at the entry point; use logging.getLogger(__name__) in modules.

code.title: Dependency inversion and a validated FastAPI endpoint
code.explain: load_data depends on a DataSource abstraction (CSV and SQL sources swap freely); extracted scale_features with a named threshold; a /v1/predict endpoint returns 200 for valid input and 422 with field errors otherwise.
mistakes: Validating inside the model code instead of at the API boundary.
code.notes: Run with: uvicorn ex2_solid_and_api:app --reload, then open /docs.
code.code:
"""Refactoring with dependency inversion, then serving behind a validated FastAPI endpoint.

load_data() depends on an abstraction (DataSource), so SQL, CSV or S3 sources can be
swapped without touching it. A Pydantic schema rejects bad requests with HTTP 422
before they reach the model. FastAPI's TestClient calls the app in-process.
"""
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
import io, csv
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

# ---- Dependency inversion ------------------------------------------------
class DataSource(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def get_all(self) -> list[dict]: ...

class CSVSource(DataSource):
    def __init__(self, text): self.text = text
    def get_all(self): return list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(self.text)))

class InMemorySQLSource(DataSource):            # stands in for a database
    def __init__(self, rows): self.rows = rows
    def get_all(self): return [dict(r) for r in self.rows]

def load_data(source: DataSource) -> list[dict]:
    return source.get_all()                     # high-level code depends on the abstraction

OUTLIER_THRESHOLD = 3.0                          # replaced magic number
def scale_features(rows):                        # extracted function (single responsibility)
    ages = [float(r["age"]) for r in rows]; mu = sum(ages) / len(ages)
    sd = (sum((a - mu) ** 2 for a in ages) / len(ages)) ** 0.5 or 1
    return [{**r, "age_z": (float(r["age"]) - mu) / sd} for r in rows if abs((float(r["age"]) - mu) / sd) < OUTLIER_THRESHOLD]

for src in [CSVSource("age,income\n34,52000\n51,61000\n29,38000"), InMemorySQLSource([{"age": 44, "income": 70000}, {"age": 23, "income": 31000}])]:
    rows = scale_features(load_data(src))
    print(f"{type(src).__name__:<18} -> {len(rows)} rows, first age_z = {rows[0]['age_z']:+.2f}")

# ---- Model as a service ---------------------------------------------------
class InputData(BaseModel):
    age: int = Field(..., gt=0, lt=120)
    income: float = Field(..., ge=0)
    zip_code: str = Field(..., min_length=5, max_length=6)

app = FastAPI(title="Churn API")

@app.post("/v1/predict")
def predict(data: InputData):
    score = min(0.99, max(0.01, 0.9 - data.income / 150000 + (0.2 if data.age < 30 else 0)))
    return {"churn_probability": round(score, 3), "class": "churn" if score > 0.5 else "stay"}

client = TestClient(app)
for payload in [{"age": 27, "income": 30000, "zip_code": "560001"},
                {"age": 150, "income": 30000, "zip_code": "560001"},
                {"age": 40, "income": "lots", "zip_code": "56"}]:
    r = client.post("/v1/predict", json=payload)
    body = r.json()
    msg = body if r.status_code == 200 else [f"{e['loc'][-1]}: {e['msg']}" for e in body["detail"]]
    print(r.status_code, msg)
print("OpenAPI docs generated at /docs; paths:", list(client.get("/openapi.json").json()["paths"]))
